title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
R Package

The primary package for spatial point patterns in R is spatstat.
spatstat uses three core custom classes:

ppp: Point Pattern (coordinates + marks).
owin: Observation Window (study boundaries).
im: Pixel Image (covariates or kernel densities).



spatstat is a massive, incredibly powerful package. It separates the point locations (ppp) from the boundary window (owin) because boundary shape affects Ripley’s K calculations and requires edge corrections.










Spatstat is one of the best maintained packages in ecology — Baddeley, Rubak & Turner’s book (2015) is the 1000-page reference if anyone gets serious.
Worth showing because error messages will sometimes name a sub-package rather than spatstat, and students find that confusing. - The book also used rgdal::readOGR to load a boundary shapefile. That’s retired; use sf::st_read() then as.owin(), or build the owin from coordinates as we do.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The Prickly Pear Cactus

Cactus species Opuntia humifusa mapped in a 50x50m plot in Florida.
Herbivore: Coreid bug (Chelinidea vittiger), a specialist insect herbivore.
Covariate: Continuous matrix vegetation height (mapped at 2m spacing).


We’ll use a simulated representation of the Florida cactus plot to demonstrate spatstat syntax. Notice that we define the boundary as a 50x50 owin.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Simulate patterns









outer(X, Y, FUN) builds every combination of the two input vectors and applies FUN to all of them at once, returning a matrix. The result has length(X) rows and length(Y) columns. So here you get a matrix with one row per value of gy and one column per value of gx
outer(gy, gx, f) produces rows indexed by gy, which is what im() wants. spatstat’s im() expects rows = y, columns = x.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
An inhomogeneous Thomas process










Thomas Process: Offspring are distributed around parents using a bivariate normal (Gaussian) distribution.

Let’s say vegetation has a positive clustering effect. We built the Thomas process rather than calling rThomas(), because: First, it makes the generative model visible: parents from a Poisson process, offspring Gaussian around them. Second, rThomas() only takes a constant parent intensity, and we want parent intensity to depend on vegetation.
So we know two true facts: clustering at scale 3.7 m, and a positive vegetation effect.
Offspring landing outside the window are dropped, which is why npoints is a bit below kappa * mu * area. Print it so students see the realized n.
cactus_ppp <- rThomas(kappa=0.015, scale=4, mu=4, win=cactus_win)
Our local 0-50 coordinates sidestep that entirely — worth mentioning as a practical tip: rescale before fitting trend models.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Visualization
First-order density can be estimated using a kernel smoother with a specified bandwidth.









summary() gives n, the average intensity, and the window. The density plot is the first-order view — where are points dense? Bright patches suggest the homogeneity assumption is shaky, which motivates Lab D. Choice of sigma matters and is arbitrary; try 1 and 6 to see. Kernel smoothing shows us areas of high local density. However, is this density variation due to small-scale clustering (second-order) or a broad environmental gradient (first-order)? Point process models will help us disentangle this.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Quadrat counts and a chi-square test
text:
Quadrat counts and a chi-square test









A significant result means the counts are inconsistent with a homogeneous Poisson process AT THE QUADRAT SCALE YOU CHOSE. Say that qualification out loud.
This is closer to a first-order analysis, since it’s about dispersion of points among sampling quadrats rather than inter-point distances. It tells you nothing about the scale of pattern.
Live demo if you have time: rerun with nx = 2 and nx = 8 and watch the p-value move. That’s the modifiable areal unit problem, and it’s the argument for the functional statistics coming next.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
K and L, ignoring edges









Three views of the same information. Panel (a) shows why nobody plots raw K — the expected curve is a parabola.
The dashed line is the theoretical CSR expectation; spatstat labels it “Kpois” or “Lpois”. The solid line is the estimate.
Panel (c) uses the formula interface . - r ~ r, which subtracts r from every curve to put the expectation at zero. That’s the second linearization convention from earlier, and it’s the one we use for the rest of the lab because departures are easiest to read against a flat line.
All three ignore edge effects, which we fix next.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: What goes wrong at the edge?
text:
What goes wrong at the edge?
Near the study area boundary you have no information about points outside.
So a circle of radius r centred near the edge contains fewer observed points than the truth.

Uncorrected statistics are therefore biased
biased increasingly at large r, because bigger circles overlap the boundary more.


The direction of bias is predictable and worth stating: uncorrected K and L will tend to DECLINE at large r, which can masquerade as regularity at large scales.
We’ll see exactly that artefact in Lab B when we compare corrected to uncorrected curves.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Edge corrections compared









Compare the three at LARGE r, where they diverge. At small r they agree, because small circles rarely touch the boundary.
The uncorrected curve should bend downward at large r. Explain why: near the edge you count fewer points than exist, so the estimate is dragged down, and the bias grows with r. That downward artefact can be misread as regularity at large scales.
Isotropic and translate should agree closely on a rectangular window. On an irregular polygon they would not, and translate is the more general choice.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Is it significant? Monte Carlo envelopes
text:
Is it significant? Monte Carlo envelopes
To test for non-randomness, we fit the L-function and compare it to Monte Carlo confidence envelopes under complete spatial randomness.

If the solid observed line climbs above the shaded gray envelope, the point pattern is statistically aggregated at those scales.










Point out how the observed solid line goes above the shaded gray envelope at distances from 2 to 12 meters. This indicates significant clustering. Ripley’s isotropic edge correction is used to weight points near the boundary.
rank = 1 means the envelope uses the min and max of the simulations. With 99 simulations that’s alpha = 0.01; with 19 it’s 0.05.
Note how much WIDER the global envelope is. That’s the multiple-testing correction: the global (simultaneous) envelope is based on the maximum deviation across all r, D = max|K(r) - Kpois(r)|, so a single excursion anywhere lets you reject.
Pointwise envelopes at a stated alpha CANNOT be used to reject the null at that alpha, because you’re testing at many distances. This is a widespread error in the published literature. Baddeley et al. (2014) and Wiegand et al. (2016) are the references; global tests are still an active area.
Report which you used. Most papers don’t.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Reading an envelope

ABOVE the band → more neighbours than the null predicts → aggregated INSIDE the band → indistinguishable from the null → no evidence against it BELOW the band → fewer neighbours than the null predicts → regular


Read the x-axis, not just the y. “Significant” is meaningless without a distance attached. The answer is always aggregated from a to b metres.
“Inside the band” is not “no pattern.” It means no pattern beyond what your null already contains.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The pair correlation function









Expectation under CSR is 1, not 0 — different from L. Mark the line.
The stoyan argument sets the smoothing kernel bandwidth coefficient; default 0.15 follows Stoyan & Stoyan (1994). Raising it to 0.4 gives a less wiggly curve. That is a real analytical choice, and the wiggliness at small r in the left panel is data sparseness, not biology.
The key comparison to make out loud: g should show aggregation concentrated at SHORT distances, while L showed it extending further. The book’s numbers are L aggregated over roughly 2-13 m, g concentrated at 2-6 m. The difference is cumulation, not signal.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The G function









Note the r axis is much SHORTER than for L or g. That’s inherent — nearest neighbour distances are by definition the shortest distances in the pattern.
correction = "rs" is the reduced-sample correction; edge handling for G works differently from K and L.
Overlaying the empirical ecdf of nndist() is a useful sanity check that spatstat is computing what you think. They should coincide.
The book’s result: nearest-neighbour distances random at very small scales (< 2 m) but closer than expected at larger scales — consistent with aggregation but with a minimum spacing, which makes biological sense for a plant with physical size.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Three functions, three answers



Function
What it said




L(r)
aggregation across a broad span of r


g(r)
aggregation concentrated at short distances


G(r)
near-random at the very smallest r, aggregated beyond




Reporting only K, or only nearest-neighbour distance, hides structure.
The G result at very small r is the interesting one: physical objects cannot overlap, so there’s an inhibition floor underneath the clustering. Two processes at two scales, and only G sees the smaller one.
Velázquez et al. (2016) audited practice and found most ecological papers use one statistic. Assign that reading with this slide in mind.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Use-availability
Chelinidea vittiger is a specialist herbivore on Opuntia. A poor disperser that shows aggregated distributions on cactus.
We want the distribution of the herbivore given the underlying distribution of cactus.
That’s a marked point pattern problem.

Here is our second player… READ THEN
Our simulation assigns the insect mark COMPLETELY AT RANDOM among cactus points, so we know the truth: no insect aggregation beyond the host plant’s.
Frame this as the availability problem. The insect can only be where cactus is. So “are insects clustered?” is nearly meaningless — of course they are, because their host is.
The right question conditions on availability. Lancaster & Downes (2004) is the methods reference for exactly this framing.
Is the insect herbivore (Chelinidea) aggregated on specific cacti, or is its distribution simply a random sample of the available cacti? - We use Random Labeling (rlabel) to test this. - Shuffles insect “presence” marks across the fixed cactus coordinates.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Build the marked pattern









Look at each mark level separately before any bivariate analysis. split() on a marked ppp will also give you one pattern per level, but passing plot arguments through plot.splitppp is unreliable, so the two panels are drawn directly here.
In the real data the mark came from six surveys per patch, truncated to presence/absence. The book does:
Note the information thrown away by truncating counts to binary. Worth a sentence: they had abundance and reduced it to occupancy for analytical convenience.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The naive analysis









This should show aggregation. And it’s an artefact — we assigned the mark at random, so there is no insect aggregation in the truth.
The apparent clustering is entirely inherited from the cactus pattern. The null here is CSR over the whole window, but the insect could never have been uniformly distributed over the window because its host isn’t.
Wrong null, wrong answer.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Condition on availability: random labelling









If we ignore the underlying cactus distribution, the insect appears clustered. But once we condition on cactus availability, we find that the insect is distributed randomly across available cacti.


Now the observed curve should sit inside the envelope: given where cactus is, the insect is randomly distributed. Which is the truth we built in.
rlabel() shuffles the marks while holding locations fixed — that is the null “insects occupy cacti at random.” rshift() is the alternative, performing a toroidal shift of one mark’s pattern while holding the other constant, which is the right null for a joint distribution question like competition between two species.
The book uses Lcross with random labelling here. Their call is envelope(ppp.PA, Lcross, nsim = 99, rank = 1, I = “presence”, …) with a CAPITAL I. Lcross takes lowercase i and j, so I lands in … and i silently defaults to the first mark level, alphabetically “absence”. The code does not analyse what the text says it analyses. Mine subsets explicitly to avoid the whole class of problem.
Worth flagging for anyone writing their own summary function: envelope() insists that fun accept an r argument or .... That is not fussiness. envelope computes the observed curve, reads the r grid off it, and passes that same grid to every simulation so the curves can be stacked. If you hardcode r inside your function instead of exposing it, envelopeEngine() stops with “‘fun’ should have an argument named ‘r’”.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Conclusion
Analyse the insect alone → aggregated
Analyse the insect conditional on cactus → random
Same data. The difference is the null model.

If you don’t control for resource availability, you’ll conclude the herbivore is highly aggregated. But the herbivore is actually just going where the cacti are. When you shuffle insect presence across the fixed cacti coordinates, the observed pattern falls inside the envelope!
Generalize it: whenever your points can only occur on a subset of the study area, CSR over the whole area is the wrong null. Nest sites can only be in trees. Camera detections can only be at camera locations. Captures can only be at traps.
That last one is directly relevant to the SCR work in this room — and it’s why SCR models condition on trap locations rather than treating detections as a free point pattern.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Continuous marks: is size clustered?









Expectation is 1. Above 1 means large cacti near other large cacti; below 1 means large near small, i.e. an inhibition or size-asymmetry process.
We assigned area independently of location, so the curve should sit inside the envelope — matching the book’s finding of no strong spatial pattern in cactus size.
Worth asking what a real positive result would mean biologically: shared favourable microsite, or age structure from clonal spread. And what a negative would mean: asymmetric competition, where a big plant suppresses its neighbours.
Recall the variogram connection — swap m_i*m_j for (m_i - m_j)^2 and this becomes essentially next week’s tool.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
A GLM for points
An inhomogeneous point process model models the intensity of points:
\[\lambda(s) = \exp(\alpha + \beta x(s) + \dots)\]

If a point pattern varies across environmental gradients, we can model it like a spatial Poisson regression using the ppm function. - We model point intensity as a function of coordinates (Easting/Northing) or environmental rasters (e.g., vegetation height)
Formally very close to Poisson regression (Illian et al. 2008; Renner et al. 2015).
Uses: exploratory analysis, inference, and prediction/mapping.
The log link is what makes it Poisson-regression-like and guarantees positive intensity.
MaxEnt is equivalent to a Poisson point process model — so presence-only SDMs ARE inhomogeneous point process models, whether or not their users know it.
Flag that now; it reframes SDMs from a machine-learning trick into a statistical model with assumptions you can check.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Fit models









The ppm function is the point pattern equivalent of a GLM. By comparing AIC, we can see if adding spatial trends or environmental covariates significantly improves our explanation of the point pattern’s first-order intensity.
We built a positive vegetation effect into the simulation, so the vegetation model should be well supported. If it isn’t, the effect size (0.10 in the simulation) is too small relative to n — worth saying out loud, because that’s a power lesson rather than a bug.
The book’s table: intercept 762.87, x+y 761.06, quadratic 753.31, vegetation 754.89. Quadratic best, vegetation close behind. With real data you can’t tell whether the quadratic is capturing vegetation indirectly or something else. With our simulation we know.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Predictions









These are fitted INTENSITY surfaces — expected points per unit area. Compare them to the kernel density plot from Lab A: the density estimate is descriptive, these are model-based.
The vegetation coefficient should be positive, recovering the 0.10 we built in. Check the magnitude — it won’t be exactly 0.10 because our covariate enters the PARENT intensity, and the offspring process smears it.
That’s a genuinely instructive mismatch: the fitted model is not the generating model. A Poisson point process model assumes independence, and a Thomas process violates it. The point estimate can still be reasonable while the standard errors are too small.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Dispersion









Linhom is the inhomogeneous L, and the null now simulates from the FITTED trend rather than from CSR. So the question changes from “is this clustered?” to “is this clustered beyond what the trend explains?”
Because our truth is a Thomas process — real clustering at 3.7 m ON TOP OF the covariate trend — some aggregation should survive. The book finds its clustering “largely (but not entirely) accounted for.”
Compare directly to the CSR envelope from Lab B: the excursion should shrink but not vanish. That contrast is the payoff of the whole lab.
This is the general recipe: control for known drivers, then ask what pattern remains. It’s the point-pattern analogue of adding covariates to a regression.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Two cluster processes









Both processes start the same way: parent points from a Poisson process, then offspring clustered around each parent.
They differ only in the offspring kernel. Matern scatters offspring UNIFORMLY within radius r of the parent — a hard edge. Thomas scatters them with an isotropic Gaussian — no hard edge, thinner tails.
Biological reading: Thomas looks like seed dispersal from a parent plant, which is why it fits the cactus data. Matern looks more like a process with a definite territory radius.
Panel (a) makes the distinction visible in one plot; the hard shoulder on the Matern kernel is the whole difference.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Fitting a cluster process as the null
text:
Fitting a cluster process as the null









kppm fits a cluster process by minimum contrast. The printout gives the cluster parameters: kappa (parent intensity), scale (sigma), and mu (mean cluster size).
Compare those to what we simulated: kappa 0.008, scale 3.7, mu 4.6. Recovery won’t be exact — minimum contrast estimation is noisy on ~90 points, and our parent intensity was inhomogeneous while kppm assumes it’s constant.
The book’s fit on real data gave mean cluster size 4.6 points at scale 3.7 m, which is where our simulation parameters came from. So this slide closes the loop.
Note you can add covariates: kppm(cactus ~ polynom(x, y, 2), “Thomas”) fits clustering AND trend together, which is the better model for our data.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Envelopes under a cluster null









The observed curve should now sit inside both envelopes: the pattern is not distinguishable from either cluster process. Which is right — we generated it from a Thomas process.
Note the envelopes are much WIDER than the CSR envelope in Lab B. A cluster process null already contains clustering, so it takes much stronger evidence to reject it.
The deeper point, and it’s Wiegand et al. (2013)’s argument: our pattern is consistent with Thomas AND with Matern. Two different generative mechanisms, one pattern. Fitting a null well is not evidence that the null is the true mechanism.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Simulating point processes









intensity() pulls lambda straight from the data, so the simulations match the observed density. Passing an im instead of a number gives an inhomogeneous process.
Emphasize what this is for. Every envelope in this deck was built from simulations exactly like these — that’s what the Monte Carlo machinery is doing under the hood. Making it explicit demystifies it.
Also: this is how you do a power analysis for a point pattern study. Simulate the effect you expect at the sample size you can afford, and see whether your statistic detects it. Nobody does this. Everybody should.
Kery & Royle (2016) is the reference for simulation-based model checking in ecology more broadly.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Recommendations
From the review you’re reading this week:

Use more than one second-order statistic — K, L, g, G to capture different information
Adjust for edge effects in almost all situations
Consider the potential for inhomogeneous patterns
Treat pointwise envelopes carefully; consider global envelopes
Remember CSR is a reference, not a hypothesis about biology


This is the practical checklist. If they internalize five things from this chapter, these are the five.
Point 4 is the one most often violated in print, and the easiest to fix.
Point 5 is the conceptual one. Rejecting CSR is nearly free — almost nothing in nature is CSR. The interesting work starts with a null that encodes something you actually believe.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Take home

The window is part of the data — change it and you change every statistic
K is cumulative; g localizes scale; G sees only the nearest neighbour
Edge effects bias you downward at large r, mimicking regularity
The null model carries the biology. Insects looked aggregated until we conditioned on their host plant
Presence-only data are thinned point data


Point 4 - If a student can articulate why the insect result changed, they’ve understood point pattern analysis better than most published users of it.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Exercise 1: Evaluate a Clustered Pattern against CSR
text:
Exercise 1: Evaluate a Clustered Pattern against CSR







Exercise 1


Generate a random Poisson process and a clustered Thomas process. Fit the G-function (nearest neighbor distance) for both and compare their curves.













The G-function rises very rapidly at small distances for clustered patterns because points are crowded close to their neighbors. Encourage students to compare this plot to the G-function of the ppp_random to see the difference.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Exercise 2: Fit and Predict an Inhomogeneous PPM
text:
Exercise 2: Fit and Predict an Inhomogeneous PPM







Exercise 2


Fit a spatial trend model to the simulated cactus dataset. Predict and map the estimated trend across the plot.













Have students change ~ x to ~ x + y or ~ polynom(x, y, 2) to see how the predicted intensity map becomes more flexible and adapts to local clustering of the points.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Roadmap for today

Point pattern and point process
Spatial randomness
Point pattern analysis


Last week, we worked with grid cells, this week we work with point locations as data and try to model how points are distributed in space. An insect that looks strongly aggregated turns out to be randomly distributed once you condition on where its host plant is.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point data

Distinct locations in space

Point data are among the most common spatial data types in ecology:

individual trees
bird nests
habitat patches
patchy disturbances such as burrows
locations of species occurrence
origin points of an invasion


Point data refers to distinct locations in space. One of the most common data types we see in spatial ecology. What are some of your point data? Camera deployments, nest sites, capture locations, telemetry fixes — though telemetry needs care, since repeated locations of one animal are not independent points.
Note the third one: habitat PATCHES as points. A patch mosaic can be reduced to a point pattern of patch centroids

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point pattern

A set of spatial coordinates of discrete “events” or individuals observed inside a specified boundary.

Typical point pattern analysis questions:

Are the points aggregated, uniform, or random?

Does that change with scale?
What process produced it?


Emphasize that PPA differs from standard spatial modeling because the point location itself is the random event under study, rather than just the attribute value at that location. We want to know: why are the points where they are?
Question 3 is the hard one, and the honest answer is often “several processes could have.”
Emphasize that 1 and 2 are descriptive and largely solved; 3 is inferential and mostly not.
Wiegand et al. (2013) is the key citation: different point processes can produce nearly identical summary statistics, which is why they argue several statistics should always be used. That paper is the reason this chapter teaches four functions instead of one.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Three processes, one pattern
How to disentangle dispersal, habitat heterogeneity, and plant-plant interactions as causes of conspecific aggregation? (Lara-Romero et al. 2016 on canvas) 

Do you have pets? Let’s say you go home and as soon as you open the door you see a broken vase on the floor. You realize that the window is open and your cat is sitting close by licking its paw. Now, all you see is a broken vase, maybe a draft blew a curtain into it, maybe the cat knocked it over, maybe someone broke in, you don’t recall if you left the window open. The pattern is the broken vase, the process could be any of these. Remmeber we talked about plants grouptogether in clusters? Using point pattern analysis we can model the underlying processes. The alternatives are: - a homogeneous point pattern process where seess are distributed at random without env preference or autocorrelation with where the trees are - Inhomogeneous poisson process where clustering is because of soil nutrients or microhabitat conditions, entirely environmental drive - Poisson cluser process where the pattern is purely as a result of dispersal from original trees - the biological process -Finally, an inhomogeneous poisson cluster process which is a combination of both biological and env.
We’ll walk through both univariate and marked point pattern analysis. We’ll be using the spatstat, which is the most comprehensive point pattern analysis package in the R ecosystem.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Spatial dispersion

The arrangement of points in space relative to one another


Aggregated (clumped): Points cluster together
Random: Points are distributed independently.
Regular (uniform): Points are evenly spaced.


library(spatstat)   # startup banner suppressed via message: false

W1 <- owin(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
set.seed(3)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(rMatClust(25, 0.05, 4, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2, 
     main = "(a) aggregated")

plot(rpoispp(100, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2, 
     main = "(c) random")

plot(rMaternII(400, 0.045, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2,  
     main = "(b) uniform (regular)")

par(op)


the three classical dispersion types. We can visually distinguish the three main forms of spatial dispersion. Panel (b) is worth pausing on — genuinely regular patterns are rare in nature and usually indicate territoriality or competition for space. - Seabloom et al. (2002, PNAS): extinction rates under non-random habitat loss differ substantially from random-loss predictions. Since real land conversion is emphatically non-random — it follows soils, slope, and roads — the standard species-area extrapolation is systematically wrong.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Dispersion is scale dependent

library(spatstat)

W1 <- owin(c(0, 1), c(0, 1))
set.seed(3)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.4, 0.5))
for (s in c(0.03, 0.08, 0.18)) {
  plot(rMatClust(12, s, 8, win = W1), pch = 19, cex = 2,
       main = paste("aggregated, scale =", s))
}
par(op)


Pattern without scale isn’t always informative. “Aggregated” without a scale attached is nearly uninformative.
at alrger scale, an aggregated pattern looks almost uniform.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Characteristics
All the methods here need x–y coordinates of point locations, plus:

a window: the study area boundary
optionally marks: attributes of points, categorical (e.g., used vs available, predator vs prey) or continuous (e.g., biomass, height)
optionally covariates: as a pixel image, e.g., elevation.


READ then: The used/unused framing is the one that generalizes best for wildlife work: your points are available resource units, and the mark says whether they were used. That converts a resource-selection question into a point pattern question (Lancaster & Downes 2004). - That’s exactly the cactus/insect example in Lab C Introduce spatstat’s three data types now, since they structure the whole lab: ppp (point pattern), owin (window), im (pixel image).
The window is the piece students underestimate, which is the next slide.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Sensitivity to window
Assumption: the pattern was generated by a single point process over the entire study area.
So the delineation of the study area, its size and location, affects the pattern you observe.
Windows can be rectangular or highly irregular polygons.

PPA is highly sensitive to the size and shape of the study boundary
This is the extent problem.
When is this assumption violated? All the time! The single-process assumption is strong and frequently violated. If half your plot is upland and half is wetland, that is arguably two processes, and pooling them will manufacture apparent aggregation that is really a habitat boundary.
Cropping to a homogeneous subregion is the crude fix. Inhomogeneous models are the solution.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point pattern information content

set.seed(11)
Wd <- owin(c(0, 10), c(0, 10))
Xd <- rMatClust(0.12, 1.1, 4, win = Wd)
n  <- npoints(Xd)

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.4, 0.5))

# (a) points in a window
plot(Xd, pch = 19, cex = 2, main = "(a) points + window (boundary)")

# (b) bivariate mark: used / unused
used <- factor(sample(c("used", "unused"), n, TRUE, prob = c(0.35, 0.65)))
plot(ppp(Xd$x, Xd$y, window = Wd, marks = used),
     cols = c("grey60", "firebrick"), chars = c(1, 19), cex = 2,
     main = "(b) bivariate mark")

# (c) continuous mark: size
sz <- rlnorm(n, log(1), 0.5)
plot(ppp(Xd$x, Xd$y, window = Wd, marks = sz),
     markscale = 0.45, main = "(c) continuous mark")

# (d) points on an underlying gradient
gg <- seq(0.1, 9.9, length.out = 60)
grad <- im(outer(gg, gg, function(yy, xx) sin(xx / 2.6) + cos(yy / 3.1)),
           xcol = gg, yrow = gg)
plot(grad, main = "(d) points on a covariate", ribbon = FALSE)
plot(Xd, add = TRUE, pch = 3, cex = 1, col = "white")
par(op)


Your point pattern could be as simple as a boundry/window and your coordinates. The points could contian categorical information such as used/unused. Or continuous information, such as group size.
Panel (b) is the resource use/availability setup. Panel (d) is the inhomogeneous case: if the covariate drives intensity, the pattern will look clustered even with no biological aggregation at all.
Panel (d) is the trap. Environmental heterogeneity and true aggregation produce the same signature in K. Distinguishing them requires either a covariate model (Lab D) or an assumption. This is the point-pattern version of the SA-env vs SA-sp distinction from Week 1’s Figure 1.2.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Poisson point process

A point process is a random process producing realizations of point patterns across space and/or time.

The most common: the Poisson point process — points are independently distributed in space, described by their intensity λ.

First-Order Intensity λ: Describes the density of points across space.
Second-Order Relationships: Relate to the spatial interaction between points (e.g., attraction, competition).


“Independently distributed” means the presence of a point at one location tells you nothing about any other location. Almost no biological process satisfies this, which is exactly why it makes a useful null.
First order: how many points, and where is density high? Second order: given a point, what’s near it?
First-order properties represent the spatial trend (large-scale density). Second-order properties represent localized interactions (small-scale clustering or competition). Intensity λ is points per unit area — roughly density. Keep the distinction between the intensity FUNCTION lambda(x), which can vary across space, and a constant lambda.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Point intensity
First-Order Intensity λ: Describes the density of points across space:

Homogeneous (= stationary) — intensity is constant across the window
Inhomogeneous (= non-stationary) — intensity varies across space

Also isotropy — the process does not change with direction.

If the density is constant across the window when Density varies across spatial or environmental gradients
When inhomogeneous, the usual objective is figuring out what explains the trend.
Stationary and homogeneous are used interchangeably here. Isotropy is the directional analogue and is almost always assumed, rarely tested.
Anisotropy is real and under-examined: patterns along a river corridor, a prevailing wind, or a contour are directional. Everything today assumes it away.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Thinned point processes

A thinned point process is one where the observed points are a sample of the underlying process.

Thinning creates inhomogeneity in the intensity function independent of the underlying process from biology (e.g., mortality) or study design.

Presence-only SDM are thinned point data (Warton & Shepherd 2010), often biased near roads, which biases model predictions (Elith et al. 2006; Phillips et al. 2009).
The logic: your MaxEnt “presence points” are a road-biased, effort-biased sample of an underlying point process. Fit a model to them and you have modelled the sampling as much as the species.
Fithian et al. (2015) is the fix — estimate the thinning process by pooling survey data with opportunistic data. Renner et al. (2015) is the general treatment.
Everything else today assumes a COMPLETE CENSUS of a region, which the cactus data is and eBird is not.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Numerical summaries

Numerical summaries are global, one number for the whole study area.

e.g., mean/variance ratio of quadrat counts, against a Poisson expectation:



Relationship
Interpretation




mean > variance
regularity


mean ≈ variance
randomness


mean < variance
aggregation



But these give no information about scale, and they are contingent on how you drew the quadrats.

The Poisson has mean equal to variance, which is why the ratio is diagnostic. Overdispersion means clustering.
“Contingent on how you drew the quadrats” is the modifiable areal unit problem again. Change the quadrat size and you change the verdict.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Functional summaries

Functional summaries are curves over distance r, which is how you get at scale.

First-order: summarize points individually, no explicit relation to other points. The intensity function λ(x).
Second-order: statistical relationships estimated from information in pairs of points. Number of points within distance r of a focal point.
Higher-order statistics exist (triplets of points) but the overwhelming majority of practice is first- and second-order.

Practical version: first order asks “where are there more points?” Second order asks “given a point here, what’s within r?” Only second-order statistics can speak to interaction, which is why they dominate.
Wiegand & Moloney (2014) cover third-order statistics for anyone curious. They exist, they’re informative, and almost nobody uses them.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Complete spatial randomness

a homogeneous Poisson process: Points occur independently with constant intensity

Two assumptions:

the number of points n in a region follows a Poisson distribution with mean λ = n/A
given n, points are an independent random sample, equally likely anywhere — uniform over the study region


Part 1 is about how many. Part 2 is about where, given how many.
“it is likely that CSR rarely occurs in nature.” It is not a biological hypothesis, it is a reference point. Rejecting CSR tells you the pattern is non-random and nothing more — it does not tell you which process produced it.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Monte Carlo envelopes
Simulate complete spatial randomness many times, at the observed n. Take the range of simulated curves as a confidence envelope (Baddeley et al. 2014).
If the observed curve falls outside, there is evidence of pattern differing from complete spatial randomness.

This is the workhorse and it is conceptually simple: build the sampling distribution of your statistic under the null by brute force.
Watch out for one thing coming in Lab B: because the envelope is computed at MANY distances r, a pointwise envelope at a stated alpha cannot be used to reject the null at that alpha. That’s a multiple-testing problem and it’s pervasive in the published literature.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Other null models

Cluster point processes — assume aggregation

Matérn Cluster: “Parent” points are random; “offspring” are distributed uniformly within a radius \(r\) around parents.
Thomas Process: Offspring are distributed around parents using a bivariate normal (Gaussian) distribution.

Inhibition processes — assume regularity

Matérn Inhibition: Points are generated but deleted if they fall within a competitive threshold distance \(r\) of another point.

Environmental gradients — use a known resource gradient as the null, then ask whether points are aggregated above and beyond it (Melles et al. 2009)


The third option is where the science is. “Are these nests clustered?” is a weak question. “Are these nests clustered beyond what the distribution of suitable substrate explains?” is a real one. inhomogeneous point process
Melles et al. (2009) did exactly this for songbird nesting — disentangling habitat drivers from social drivers of nesting pattern. Directly relevant to anyone in this room working on colonial or territorial species.
Lab D and Lab E implement both routes.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:

set.seed(21)
px <- c(5.0, 6.9, 3.3, 7.6, 4.4, 8.4, 2.4, 6.1, 3.8, 7.1)
py <- c(5.0, 6.4, 6.8, 3.6, 3.1, 6.9, 3.9, 8.1, 2.0, 5.2)

        bg = "grey92", fg = "grey40")

## (b) g : a ring at radius r, smoothed
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), asp = 1)

        bg = "grey92", fg = NA)

        bg = "white", fg = NA)

        fg = "grey35", lwd = 2)

text(px[1] + 1.7, py[1] + 0.4, "r", font = 3, cex = 2)
box(col = "grey50")

## (c) G : nearest neighbour only
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), asp = 1)
points(px, py, pch = 19, cex = 2)
points(px[1], py[1], pch = 15, cex = 2.5, col = "firebrick")
d <- sqrt((px - px[1])^2 + (py - py[1])^2); d[1] <- Inf
nnb <- which.min(d)
arrows(px[1], py[1], px[nnb], py[nnb], length = 0.12, lwd = 2.5,
       col = "firebrick")
box(col = "grey50")
title("(c) G : nearest neighbour distance", cex.main = 2)

Moving away from detecting patterns by numerical summeries, we can use functional summaries. Here are three geometries, three questions.

K uses everything inside the disc, so it is CUMULATIVE.
g uses only what’s in a thin ring at r, so it is scale-LOCAL. The grey band is the smoothing kernel bandwidth.
G uses only the single nearest neighbour, so it emphasizes the shortest distances and ignores everything else.

Ask which they’d use to detect clustering at exactly 5 m but not at 10 m. Answer is g, and the reason is the cumulative-versus-local distinction that comes up three slides on.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Ripley’s K
The degree of spatial aggregation of points within a circle of radius r, compared to complete spatial randomness:
\[K(r) = \frac{E}{\lambda}\]
where λ = n/A and E = expected number of points within r of an arbitrarily chosen point, excluding that point.

K(r) larger than expected → clustering
K(r) smaller than expected → regularity


Ripley (1976). The most-used second-order statistic in ecology by a wide margin.
“Excluding that point” matters — otherwise every point contributes itself and you’d have a constant offset.
Dividing by lambda is what makes it comparable across patterns of different density. Without that, K would just track abundance.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: K under CSR, and the r² problem
text:
K under CSR, and the r² problem
Area of a circle is πr², so under complete spatial randomness the expected count is \(E_{\text{CSR}} = \lambda \pi r^2\), giving
\[K(r)_{\text{CSR}} = \pi r^2\]
That grows quadratically, which makes plots hard to read — deviations at large r dominate visually.

This is why nobody plots raw K. The expected curve is a parabola, so eyeballing departures from it is unreliable, and the vertical scale is dominated by large r.
The fix is linearization, next slide. It’s purely cosmetic in the sense that no information changes — but it makes the plot readable, which matters.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Linearizing to L — two conventions
Expectation = r: \[\hat L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi}\] aggregation if L(r) > r; regularity if L(r) < r
Expectation = 0: \[\hat L(r) = \sqrt{K(r)/\pi} - r\] aggregation if L(r) > 0; regularity if L(r) < 0
Always check which one a figure uses.

That last line is not pedantry. Both conventions are common, both are called “L”, and reading a figure under the wrong one inverts your interpretation of where the null line sits.
spatstat’s Lest uses expectation = r. To get expectation = 0 you plot with the formula . - r ~ r, which we do throughout the lab. Point that out when it first appears.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
How K is actually computed
\[\hat K(r) = A \frac{\sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} w_{ij} \, I(d_{ij} < r)}{n^2}\]

\(d_{ij}\) — distance between points i and j
\(I(\cdot)\) — indicator, 1 if \(d_{ij} < r\), else 0
\(w_{ij}\) — weight correcting for edge effects

Ignore the weights and it simplifies to counting neighbours within r, scaled by intensity.

Strip away the notation and it’s: count all pairs closer than r, scale by density and area. That’s it.
The w term is the entire edge-correction literature compressed into one subscript, and it’s the subject of three slides from now.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The pair correlation function g
\[g(r) = \frac{dK(r)/dr}{2\pi r}\]
The slope of K at radius r, divided by the circumference at r.

g(r) = 1 → CSR
g(r) > 1 → aggregation
g(r) < 1 → regularity


Because it’s a derivative, g isolates what happens AT r rather than out to r.
In practice it’s implemented either with a ring width (delta-r) or, better, with a smoothing kernel (Penttinen et al. 1992). Bandwidth is a real choice: too narrow and data sparseness makes the curve wiggle spuriously; too wide and it approaches K.
The O-ring statistic of Wiegand & Moloney (2004) is a close relative: O(r) = lambda * g(r).

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: Why g beats K for identifying scale
text:
Why g beats K for identifying scale
K is cumulative — all points closer than r are used.
So strong aggregation at 5 m makes K look aggregated at 10 m too, because r = 10 still contains everything inside 5.
g is a derivative, so it localizes.
K is simply the cumulative version of g (Baddeley 2007; Velázquez et al. 2016).

This is the most practically useful methodological point in the chapter, and it shows up in the Lab B results: L suggests aggregation from 2-13 m, while g localizes it to 2-6 m. The L signal at 8-13 m is an artefact of cumulation.
Illian et al. (2008) recommend distance-based analyses either to complement or in place of K. Velázquez et al. (2016), one of this week’s readings, found ecologists still overwhelmingly report K.
If a paper reports only K and claims a scale, be sceptical.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
The G function
Cumulative distribution of nearest-neighbour distances. The “event-to-event” distribution.
\[\hat G(r) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbf{1}(d_i \leq r) \qquad
G(r)_{\text{CSR}} = 1 - \exp(-\lambda \pi r^2)\]

G(r) > GCSR(r) → distances shorter than expected → aggregation
G(r) < GCSR(r) → longer than expected → regularity


Intuitive: the probability of finding your nearest neighbour within distance r.
The catch: it ignores everything beyond the nearest neighbour, so it captures smaller-scale structure than K, L or g. Notice in Lab B that the r axis for G is much shorter — that’s not a plotting choice, it’s inherent.
Useful side application: G gives you a way to interpret the spatial scaling of patch isolation, connecting to nearest-neighbour distance metrics from Chapter 3.
The empty-space function F is the location-focused analogue. We skip it, as the book does.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Marks: bivariate and continuous
Bivariate (cross) K — for two categorical point types:
\[\hat K_{12}(r) = A \frac{\sum_i \sum_j I(d_{ij} < r)}{n_1 n_2}\]
computed for \(K_{12}\) and \(K_{21}\), then averaged.
Mark correlation function — for continuous marks:
\[\hat K_m(r) = \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} I_r \, m_i m_j\]
Asks whether large values tend to be near other large values.

A lovely connection the book points out: replace m_i * m_j with (m_i - m_j)^2 and the mark correlation function becomes nearly equivalent to the empirical variogram, which is Chapter 5’s central tool. Same arithmetic, different tradition.
Flag that now — it makes next week feel continuous with this week rather than a fresh start.
Interpretation for the mark correlation: above 1 means large near large, below 1 means large near small.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity overview
Format: Pairs
Materials: 2 maps, 1 distance card, ruler
Suppose you have a complete census of elk across a 2km × 2km block of the Blackfoot
Your group’s job: For each distance card, determine with numbers if elk locations on the maps are aggregated, random, or regular?

Preparation:

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 1


0 - 3 minutes. Look at Map A. In one word, please write down: Are these elk clustered, random, or regular?
2 - 4 minutes. Propose a method to prove with numbers what you committed in the previous step.



Hand out Map A and give no other instructions. Do not mention distance, scale, or nulls.
Everyone will write “clustered.” That unanimity is the setup — it means the reversal in phase 4 lands on the whole room at once rather than on one unlucky group.
Harvest proposals on the board. DO NOT EVALUATE ANY OF THEM.
This phase is supposed to be uncomfortable. Two to three minutes of genuine floundering is the goal.
EXPECT THESE PROPOSALS, and write all of them up without comment:
“Count elk in squares and see if some squares have more” -> quadrats, a real method, and the one the hook uses “Measure the distance to each elk’s nearest neighbour” -> the G function, arriving spontaneously “Compare to a map where they’re spread out evenly” -> a null model, arriving spontaneously “Calculate the average distance between all pairs”
IF NOBODY MENTIONS A COMPARISON, ask: “clustered compared to WHAT?” and let the silence do the work. That question is the whole lesson, and it is far better if the room feels the need for it before you supply an answer.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 2

Here is the measurement we will make: for a typical elk, count how many OTHER elk lie within distance r of it.
To know whether that count is a lot, you need to know what randomness would have given you.



There are 60 elk in 4 km². If those 60 elk were scattered at random across the block, how many would you expect to find inside a circle of radius r?
Work it out. You have everything you need.



DO NOT HAND THEM THE FORMULA. They will get there in about ninety seconds, and it is the last thing in this activity they can own.
The route: density = 60 / 4 = 15 elk per km². Area of a circle = pi r squared. Expected = 15 x pi r squared, with r in kilometres.
RESCUE PROMPT, if a group stalls past a minute: “if there were 15 elk per square kilometre, how many sit inside a circle of 0.28 square kilometres?” That is enough; do not finish it for them.
WATCH FOR THE UNITS TRAP. Several groups will work in metres and get an answer thousands of times too big. Let them discover it by sanity-checking against the map: a 100 m circle cannot contain 47,000 elk. Units errors caught by physical plausibility are worth more than units errors caught by you.
ONCE A GROUP HAS IT, write their formula on the board in their notation and leave it up. Phase 3 refers back to it.
STILL SAY NOTHING about scale-dependence, nulls, grain, or which map to use.
IF ASKED “which r?” -> “whichever one is on your card.” IF ASKED “which map?” -> “you decide, and be ready to justify it.”

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 3


Pick a distance (m) and follow the steps below.

Measure the scale bar on each map with your ruler. Work out how many millimetres equal one metre on each map.
Decide which map your question can be answered on. Be ready to justify it.
Pick three focal elk. For each, draw a circle of radius r and count how many other elk fall inside.
Average your three counts → observed.
Compute expected, using the formula your group just derived.
Report observed ÷ expected. That ratio is your answer.




DISTANCE CARDS: 8 m, 30 m, 100 m, 500 m — one per group.
WHAT EACH RADIUS BECOMES ON EACH MAP (for you, not for them):
       Map A        Map B
8 m 0.8 mm 8 mm 30 m 3 mm 30 mm 100 m 10 mm 100 mm 500 m 50 mm off the map
WHAT WILL HAPPEN, GROUP BY GROUP.
GROUP A (8 m) tries Map A, finds 8 m is under a millimetre, and gets stuck. LET THEM STAY STUCK FOR A FULL MINUTE before nudging: “is there another map on your desk?” That moment of being unable to ask the question is discovery 3, and it is worth the discomfort.
GROUP B (30 m) has the same experience in milder form — 3 mm is drawable but uncountable, because the herd is a smudge. They should migrate to Map B.
GROUP C (100 m) on Map B will find a 100 mm radius runs off the sheet. The elegant route is to measure the herd’s greatest dimension (60 m) and realise every 100 m circle therefore contains the entire herd, so the answer is 19 without drawing anything. If a group gets there, have them present it.
GROUP D (500 m) must use Map A, because 500 m does not exist on Map B. Their circle covers a quarter of the landscape and still contains only their own cluster.
Everyone will notice they are measuring ELK TO ELK — not to a habitat edge, not a cell size. Do not say so. Ask it in phase 6.

Activity: Phase 4
Each group reports one ratio.

So — are elk clustered?


Write only what groups report. Let the pattern emerge in front of them — build the table live rather than projecting the filled version.
DISCOVERY 1. Let the room fight about it. Someone will say “clustered at some distances and not others,” and when they do, write their sentence on the board VERBATIM and put their name next to it. That sentence is the chapter.
Only AFTER they have said it do you supply the vocabulary: dispersion is not a property of a point pattern, it is a property of a point pattern AT A STATED DISTANCE — which is why K, g and G are functions of r rather than single numbers.
DISCOVERY 3 falls out here too. Ask Group A what happened when they tried Map A. Their answer is that the question could not be asked. Extent determines which distances you have any hope of resolving.
IF THE RATIO COLUMN CONFUSES ANYONE: 1.0 means exactly as many neighbours as randomness predicts, above 1 means more, below 1 means fewer.

Project this only after the live table is built, as a check.
THREE ROWS COME FROM MAP B, ONE FROM MAP A. That is not sloppiness — which map a group CAN use is determined by their radius, and the boundary sits between 100 m and 500 m. Fill in the “From map” column as groups report, and then ask the room why the column is not all the same. The answer is discovery 3.
Every observed value is exact, because the elk sit on a 12 m lattice: a 5 by 4 grid at 12 m spacing gives mean neighbour counts of 0 at 8 m, 11.1 at 30 m, and 19 (everyone) at any r above 60 m.
Groups may be off by a neighbour or two depending on which focal elk they chose — worth naming, since it is why you average over several focal points rather than trusting one.
At 500 m the nearest elk in another herd is about 1002 m away, so a 500 m circle still contains only the group’s own cluster. Hence 19 again, but now against an expectation of 11.78 — the signal has washed out.
TWO THINGS A SHARP STUDENT WILL RAISE. Have both ready.
“MAP B ONLY SHOWS ONE OF THE THREE HERDS — how do you know the others look like it?” You don’t, from Map B alone. Groups A, B and C are all making a claim about ONE herd and generalising. Here the three herds are identical by construction, so it happens to be safe. The honest answer is that checking that assumption is exactly what a real analysis does by averaging over many focal points spread across the whole window. This is a genuinely good objection — say so.
GROUP D HAD TO USE BOTH MAPS. At 1 mm = 10 m their own herd is a 5 mm smudge, so they cannot resolve 20 dots inside it. Most groups will infer “about 20” rather than count, or go to Map B for the count and return to Map A to confirm nothing else falls within 50 mm. THAT TWO-MAP WORKFLOW IS THE RIGHT ANSWER and is worth naming out loud: Group D needed Map A for what is ABSENT at 500 m and Map B for what is PRESENT at close range. No single extent could answer their question.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 5
On Map B (one herd, 20 elk in a 180 × 180 m frame), we found zero neighbours within 8 m. Ratio equals 0, fewer than random.


Have we proved that elk avoid standing close together?



A close pair: two elk standing closer together than 8 m.
Before you can call zero a finding, you have to ask: would randomness have given us zero too?


Let them argue for a minute before you touch the arithmetic.
DEFINE “PAIR” OUT LOUD, because the next slide depends on it. Pick any two elk, measure between them; if that distance is under 8 m they are a close pair. The question is how many such pairs randomness would produce.
THE LOGIC TO LAND: if randomness also produces zero, then finding zero tells you nothing about elk. You have not measured the elk — you have measured the fact that 8 m is a very small circle.
Do not run this slide together with the next one. The pause between “you might have nothing” and “watch what happens when we change the window” is what makes the reversal land.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity: Phase 5
Work it out for Map B, 20 elk in a 180 × 180 m frame.
density = 20 ÷ 0.0324 km² = 617 elk per km²
expected neighbours per elk = 617 × π(0.008)² = 0.124
expected pairs = 20 × 0.124 ÷ 2 = 1.24 pairs

Why divide by two? Every pair got counted twice — elk A counts B as a neighbour, and B counts A.
Randomness on Map B predicts about 1.2 close pairs. You would see zero about 29% of the time.


THE DIVIDE-BY-TWO IS THE STEP PEOPLE SKIP. Make them say why.
“1.24 PAIRS” IS NONSENSE AS A LITERAL OBJECT, so explain it as a rate: scatter 20 elk at random in this frame, count the close pairs, write it down, and repeat a thousand times. You would average 1.24 pairs per attempt — which means zero happens about 29% of the time.
That framing is far more persuasive than “1.24 is a small number.” Say it as: a zero here is roughly a one-in-three outcome under the hypothesis Group A thinks they have rejected.
WHY MAP B AND NOT MAP A. Group A counted on Map B, so the expectation has to be computed for Map B. Mixing windows — observing on one map and expecting on another — is the exact error this phase teaches, and it is easy to commit by accident. If you had used the whole-block density of 15 per km2 here you would have got 0.09 pairs and a P(zero) of 91%: same conclusion, wrong arithmetic.
The 29% figure treats close-pair counts as Poisson. Fine at this magnitude.

DISCOVERY 4, and the deepest thing available in this chapter.
Build the table row by row on the board rather than projecting it. Each row is the same three-step calculation with one number changed, and watching the answer move CONTINUOUSLY with the window is the whole point — it is far better than jumping between two cherry-picked extremes.
THEN ASK THE ROOM WHICH WINDOW IS CORRECT. Let them fail to answer. That failure is the lesson: there is no principled stopping rule. The analyst picks the window, and the picking determines the finding. It is why Chapter 4 spends its length on null models rather than on statistics.
HAVE THIS READY: someone will ask why the herd box is 60 x 48 rather than 48 x 36, the exact span of the elk. Because the tight bounding box assumes elk occupy no space and inflates the density further. A tighter box gives an even stronger result — which is itself another turn of the same screw.
DO NOT EXTEND ANY OF THIS TO r = 30 m. With the herd window the formula returns 196 expected pairs from a herd that has only 190 pairs in total, because a 30 m radius does not fit inside a 60 x 48 m box. If a quick group tries it and gets nonsense, praise them — they have found an edge effect, which is Sheet D item (a) in the gauge.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Activity debrief







What we found
The name for it




The verdict changes with the distance you ask about
Dispersion is scale-dependent


We were measuring elk-to-elk distances. No pixel, no quadrat, no grain
r is the scale of analysis


We couldn’t ask the 8m question on a 2km map
Extent limits detectable scales


Same r, two densities, opposite results
The null model decides the answer




ASK, DON’T TELL. For each row, ask “what did we actually find out?”, write their words, then add the term beside it. The terms stick because they are labels for something the room already owns.
ROW 2 IS THE ONE THEY WILL NOT VOLUNTEER, so prompt it: “what two things were you measuring the distance between?” Elk and elk. “So what was the grain of this analysis?” There wasn’t one. Point patterns are the only data type in this course with NO GRAIN AT ALL, because exact coordinates mean there is no aggregation unit. Students arriving from Lessons 2 and 3 have been trained to hear every distance as grain or extent, and this is where you break it.
TWO OPTIONAL FOLLOW-UPS IF TIME REMAINS.
FIRST- VERSUS SECOND-ORDER. Which of the verdicts is about the environment and which about the elk? Three clusters a kilometre apart is FIRST-ORDER — intensity varies because habitat does, and it would hold even if elk ignored each other entirely. The 8 m spacing is SECOND-ORDER — points responding to other points, and it would happen in a perfectly uniform meadow.
PROCESS VERSUS PATTERN. “Same census tomorrow at 7 a.m. — same map?” No: different coordinates, same rules. The point PROCESS is the rule elk follow; the point PATTERN is where they happened to stand on Tuesday. You only ever observe the second and you are always trying to infer the first.


Dispersion is not a property of a point pattern; it is a property of a point pattern at a stated distance. That is why K, g, and G are functions of r rather than single numbers.
PROCESS VS PATTERN. “Fly again tomorrow at 7 a.m. — same map?” No: different coordinates, same rules. The point PROCESS is the rule elk follow; the point PATTERN is where they happened to stand on Tuesday. You only ever observe the second and you are always trying to infer the first.
Closing line: “Clustered compared to what?” is not a pedantic question. It is the entire chapter.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
section: What goes wrong at the boundary
text:
What goes wrong at the boundary
Near the study area boundary you have no information about points outside.
So a circle of radius r centred near the edge contains fewer observed points than the truth.
Uncorrected statistics are therefore biased — and biased increasingly at large r, because bigger circles overlap the boundary more.

The direction of bias is predictable and worth stating: uncorrected K and L will tend to DECLINE at large r, which can masquerade as regularity at large scales.
We’ll see exactly that artefact in Lab B when we compare corrected to uncorrected curves.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
Corrections

set.seed(8)
ex <- runif(28, 0, 10); ey <- runif(28, 0, 10)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.6, 0.6, 2.8, 0.6))

## (a) isotropic weighting
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(-4, 11), ylim = c(-2.5, 12.5), asp = 1)
symbols(8.6, 5, circles = 3.4, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE,
        bg = "grey93", fg = "grey45")
rect(0, 0, 10, 10, border = "grey25", lwd = 2)
points(ex, ey, pch = 19, cex = 0.9)
points(8.6, 5, pch = 15, cex = 1.8, col = "firebrick")
# points that would exist outside but are unobserved
points(c(11.4, 10.9, 11.8), c(4.2, 6.6, 5.4), pch = 1, cex = 1.1,
       col = "grey55")
text(0.2, 11.6, "(a) isotropic weighting", adj = 0, cex = 1.15, font = 2)
text(-3.8, -1.9, "w = 1 / (fraction of\ncircumference inside)",
     adj = 0, cex = 0.95)

## (b) toroidal shift
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(-4, 11), ylim = c(-2.5, 12.5), asp = 1)
rect(0, 0, 10, 10, border = "grey25", lwd = 2)
points(ex, ey, pch = 19, cex = 0.9)
# wrapped copies
points(ex - 10, ey, pch = 1, cex = 0.7, col = "grey60")
points(ex, ey + 10, pch = 1, cex = 0.7, col = "grey60")
arrows(9.4, 11.1, 0.6, 11.1, length = 0.11, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
arrows(-1.2, 0.6, -1.2, 9.4, length = 0.11, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
text(0.2, 11.9, "(b) translate / toroidal shift", adj = 0, cex = 1.15,
     font = 2)
text(-3.8, -1.9, "wrap the plot onto a torus;\nno weights needed",
     adj = 0, cex = 0.95)
par(op)


Isotropic (Ripley 1988): if the circle is entirely inside, w = 1. If half the circumference is outside, w = 2 for points inside. Intuitive, but works poorly for irregular complex boundaries.
Translate (toroidal): wrap the window like a torus so the pattern has no edge. Works on ALL window geometries, which is why it’s the general-purpose default and what we use in the lab.
The open circles in (a) are the points you don’t get to see. That’s the whole problem in one visual.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
When not to correct
If the boundary is a hard, true boundary for the points, correcting is wrong (Lancaster & Downes 2004).
Examples: a pond edge for aquatic larvae; an island coastline; a fenced enclosure.
The correction assumes points could exist outside. Sometimes they can’t.

Good discussion prompt: is your study plot boundary real or arbitrary? Almost always arbitrary, which is why correction is almost always right — but the exceptions matter and nobody thinks about them.
A stream reach for benthic insects, a habitat patch boundary for a specialist, a lake shore. In those cases the “missing” points genuinely do not exist and inflating your counts invents them.

title: WILD 591 – Spatial Population Modeling
text:
What all of this assumes

Stationarity (homogeneity) — intensity constant over space
Isotropy — no directional dependence
Complete census, not a sample

The functions can be extended to inhomogeneous processes (Lab D). Isotropy usually just gets assumed.
On sampling: randomly thinning a Poisson process leaves a Poisson process, so random samples are defensible. Biased samples are not.

That last point is subtle and worth stating carefully. Random thinning preserves Poisson-ness, so a random subsample doesn’t invalidate a CSR test. Systematic or biased thinning does.
Which brings back the presence-only problem: road-biased occurrence records are biased, not random, thinning. Everything today would be invalid on them.
